summary: Intro discovery call focused on architecture tradeoffs for retrieval + rerank at Sable Therapeutics. Primary constraints: health-care data residency, VPC-only deployments, and high QPS (~3k qps peak) with low median latency for clinical search. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, vector DB integration patterns (sidecar vs external), sharding strategies, embedding dimensionality and rerank CPU cost. Agreed next steps to run a Dedicated throughput benchmark and exchange sample data.
topics: Vector DB integration patterns (managed vs co-located)
Embedding dimensionality tradeoffs and rerank latency
Fallback and hybrid search strategies (sparse + dense)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-15 14:30 PST — Duration 58m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Rajiv (Head of ML, Sable), Hannah (Infra), Tom (CTO)
---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll dive into your retrieval and rerank constraints. Rajiv, do you want to kick off with what you're trying to solve?
[00:12] Rajiv (Customer): Yeah, sure. So the short version, we have a clinical knowledge base — about 250k documents right now — and the ask is low-latency, high-accuracy retrieval for clinicians. They want near real-time, like median under 150ms for the top-k retrieve+rerank path, and peaks of maybe 3k qps during morning rounds.
[00:32] Hannah (Customer): And to add, anything we run has to be in our VPC or on-prem — we can't put PHI outside our environment. So Hosted only is unlikely unless you have a VPC/private offering.
[00:44] Maya: Totally. We'll map that to Redwood Private / Dedicated options. Ethan, do you want to say a little about our deployment patterns for vector DB integrations?
[00:50] Ethan (Redwood SE): Yeah, thanks. A couple of common architectures: 1) Redwood manages the model inference and you push embeddings to a managed VDB like Pinecone or Qdrant; 2) Co-located model + VDB in the same VPC — either the customer runs the DB and we talk to it over private network, or we deploy an on-prem agent; 3) Sidecar pattern where embedding generation is colocated next to the app and we only handle the rerank/LLM calls. Each has tradeoffs for latency and throughput.
[01:23] Rajiv: For us, co-located is favored. We don't want any cross-Internet hops — so either Redwood in our VPC or a private deployment. Also curious about the sharding story — how would you scale to 3k qps?
[01:36] Ethan: Scaling is mostly orthogonal: vector DB sharding + Redwood Dedicated compute for rerank. For retrieval we recommend sharding the vector index by document hash across nodes or regions, and for rerank we can run batched candidate scoring on Dedicated GPU or CPU pools depending on model choice. We also support prefix/K-V caching for repeated queries to hit latency SLOs.
[01:55] Hannah: Can you explain K-V cache? Is that the KV cache for decoder states or something else?
[02:02] Ethan: Sorry, yes, I mean prefix and KV-cache for LLM generation; for retrieval we also cache top-N candidates for hot queries. Sometimes the transcript system hears K-V as K-V cash — apologies if earlier notes are off.
[02:16] Tom (CTO): What's the cost delta between Hosted and Dedicated for a workload like ours? Ballpark.
[02:22] Maya: Hosted is typically simpler and cheaper at low volume, but given you need VPC and sustained throughput, Dedicated or Private makes sense. We'll send a cost matrix, but as an example, a 4-GPU Dedicated pool optimized for rerank at 3k qps sustained will have a different pricing profile — you'll see savings once you commit monthly. We'll follow up with numbers.
[02:44] Rajiv: On embeddings — we're using a 1536-dim dense vector today (open model), but considering 1024 or even 768 if we can keep rerank quality. Thoughts?
[02:55] Ethan: Dimensionality is a tradeoff: higher dims = higher disk/RAM usage and slower nearest-neighbor, but often better zero-shot recall. For rerank, a smaller embedding plus an aggressive reranker can match higher-dim recall for many cases. If you're willing to do a hybrid approach — sparse BM25 + 768-d dense — you often get good results with smaller index footprints.
[03:18] Hannah: If we go smaller dims, does that reduce CPU/GPU cost for rerank?
[03:24] Ethan: Rerank cost is mostly proportional to number of candidates and the model used for rerank rather than embedding dim. Smaller embedding helps retrieval latency and index memory, but rerank model time is about scoring N candidates — if you reduce top-N you reduce cost. We recommend testing 64‑128 candidates for rerank and measuring downstream latency.
[03:44] Rajiv: Our current pipeline: embeddings stored in Milvus, retrieval returns top-200, then a BERT-style rerank on CPU. That sometimes hits 400-600ms which is too slow for clinicians. We're exploring moving the rerank to GPU.
[04:00] Ethan: Moving rerank to GPU and batching is a common win. Redwood Dedicated supports continuous batching for rerank scoring — we can batch requests into micro-batches to keep tail latency low. The trick is tuning batch sizes vs SLOs.
[04:15] Maya: Also worth noting, we have automatic fallback policies so if Dedicated pool is hot, we can degrade to a smaller model or fail over to a cached response. That helps availability.
[04:29] Tom: Regarding regulatory — we need audit logs, KMS for keys, and SSO integration. You support SAML/SSO and customer-managed KMS?
[04:38] Maya: Yes. For Private and Dedicated we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations (customer-managed keys). We also produce audit logs with token-level tracing in the Console. We'll attach the SOC2 whitepaper and details.
[04:51] Rajiv: Could you run a baseline throughput test with our Milvus dataset? We can provide a 5k query sample.
[04:58] Ethan: Absolutely. For benchmarking we need: sample vectors (or the service endpoint and credentials), a query trace (5k queries with timing distribution), and candidate counts to score. We'll run it on a 4-GPU Dedicated profile first and report latency percentiles and cost per 1M queries.
[05:15] Hannah: Network-wise, we need to keep traffic inside our VPC. How does your private deployment connect?
[05:21] Ethan: Two options: 1) Redwood Private with control plane peered and data plane inside customer VPC via a managed connector; 2) On-prem package where the inference runtime runs inside your infra, and Redwood control plane is optional. Both allow KMS and audit logs to be on-prem or forwarded to your SIEM.
[05:36] Rajiv: For the vector DB, is it better to have Milvus co-located and allow Redwood to request over private network, or do you recommend moving index into Redwood-managed store inside our VPC?
[05:47] Ethan: Co-locating Milvus is common — you keep ownership and avoid data movement. Redwood will call into your Milvus via internal network. Alternatively, if you want Redwood-managed indexes in your VPC we can run our index service in your VPC with RBAC. The key considerations: network latency, operational ownership, backup/DR.
[06:03] Tom: What about hybrid search — BM25 + dense? Implementation complexity?
[06:07] Ethan: It's straightforward: you run a sparse prefilter (BM25) to get a candidate set, then dense retrieval or rerank. Some vector DBs support hybrid queries natively; otherwise you can do two-step: sparse engine returns top-M, then dense/ann returns top-N from those. This reduces candidate set size and thus rerank cost.
[06:26] Rajiv: Our current top-N is 200 which is heavy. We could try BM25 prefilter to 500 then dense to 100 then rerank 50.
[06:35] Maya: Sounds like a good test. For the benchmark, include a couple of candidate pipelines so we can compare cost/latency/quality.
[06:42] [short crosstalk — someone drops audio for a second]
[07:00] Rajiv: A few specific questions: do you support quantized embeddings storage? And second, do you have any recommendations for approximate NN engine choice for high-dim vectors?
[07:10] Ethan: For storage you can use quantized indexes (IVFPQ, OPQ) depending on the VDB; that reduces memory. For ANN engines, HNSW is common for recall at small GPU counts, but for distributed high-QPS we look at sharded IVF variants. We'll share a short doc comparing HNSW vs IVF vs PQ for your size.
[07:28] Tom: If we quantize aggressively, what's the quality hit?
[07:31] Ethan: Usually small if you tune params; the reranker can often recover quality loss. We recommend end-to-end evals.
[07:38] Rajiv: On the rerank model, are you recommending a GPU-optimized small transformer or something like a distilled BERT on CPU?
[07:47] Ethan: For latency targets under 150ms end-to-end, GPU-accelerated transformer rerankers with batching are the fastest. Distilled CPU models are cheaper but have higher tail latency. With Dedicated you can choose per-route allocations.
[07:59] Maya: Quick poll — is a pilot scope a 2-week Dedicated benchmark followed by a 4-week POC with 95th percentile SLO targets? Rajiv?
[08:07] Rajiv: Yes, that sounds reasonable. We'll need to define success criteria: median <150ms, p95 <350ms for clinician queries, and retrieval recall delta <2% vs baseline.
[08:18] Hannah: Also we need to exercise failover — what happens when a Dedicated pool is overloaded.
[08:24] Ethan: We have automated rollbacks and fallback policies. For overloaded pools you can fallback to a cheaper model or return cached responses. We can simulate load during the benchmark.
[08:34] Tom: Any network egress concerns? If Redwood in our VPC calls our Milvus, is there any egress billing on your side?
[08:42] Maya: If everything stays inside your VPC and we use private peering, no public egress. We'll provide a networking diagram in the follow-up.
[08:49] [10m silence marker skipped]
[09:01] Rajiv: Let's talk security review — we run quarterly audits. We need logs to be forwarded to Splunk and proof of SOC2 compliance.
[09:09] Maya: We'll hand you the SOC2 report sections and details about audit log exports. For Splunk, we support log forwarding, and we can do a checklist for the security team.
[09:17] Rajiv: Great. For the benchmark data, we'll redact PHI but keep clinical structure. Can you sign an NDA or provide an MSA addendum?
[09:26] Maya: We can start with a mutual NDA; for PII/PHI we can execute the data addendum. I'll coordinate with legal.
[09:34] [Timestamp jumps — mid-call deeper technical dive with Ethan]
[12:12] Ethan: For the rerank batching strategy: we do continuous batching with dynamic batch size. If you have steady QPS we can fill batches efficiently and keep GPU utilization high; for spiky traffic we provision autoscale and burst capacity. Important tuning knobs: target latency bucket, max batch size, and max wait time.
[12:33] Hannah: How do you measure per-route token usage and cost? We need token-level attribution for billing to teams.
[12:40] Maya: The Console shows token-level breakdown per route and model; you can tag routes to chargeback teams. We'll demo in the follow-up.
[12:48] Rajiv: A nit — you mentioned KV cache earlier. Are you caching embedding vectors or the rerank model outputs?
[12:54] Ethan: Both patterns exist: caching top candidates for hot queries (embedding-level cache), and caching rerank scores for exact queries. Cache invalidation is application-specific.
[13:06] Tom: Operational question: what's failure recovery like if a node dies mid-rerank batch?
[13:12] Ethan: We checkpoint KV cache and we have retry policies. For a node failure we re-route to healthy nodes and attempt partial retries; the system is designed to avoid long head-of-line blocking.
[13:23] Rajiv: Any guidance for index refreshes in Milvus? We update docs weekly.
[13:29] Ethan: For frequent updates we recommend nearline pipelines where you do incremental indexing and background merges. Full reindex is expensive. If you have heavy write rates, consider append-only shards with periodic compaction.
[13:41] Maya: OK we have about 20 minutes left — should we sketch the pilot plan now?
[13:46] Rajiv: Yes.
[13:47] Maya: Pilot outline: 1) Send sample queries and vectors (customer). 2) SE runs Dedicated 4-GPU benchmark with three candidate pipelines (pure dense 1536dim, hybrid BM25+768 dense, quantized 1024dim with IVF). 3) Measure median/p95/p99 latencies for retrieve+rerank, recall metrics, and cost estimates. 4) Security runbook + network diagram. 5) Decision meeting. Does that capture it?
[14:18] Hannah: Yes. Add load-failure simulation.
[14:21] Maya: Added. Any questions about timeline? We suggested starting bench week of 12/18 and follow-up week of 12/22.
[14:29] Rajiv: That works. One more item — for rerank model export, can you run ONNX or do you need a native model?
[14:36] Ethan: We accept ONNX and TorchScript; we also have optimized kernels for certain transformers. We'll take whatever you can provide.
[14:43] Tom: Who's the day-to-day Redwood contact?
[14:46] Maya: Primary is me for AE and Ethan for SE. I'll set up a slack invite to the pilot channel.
[14:52] Rajiv: Cool.
[15:00] [closing recap]
[15:05] Maya: Recap: Redwood to share Dedicated pricing + SOC2 + network diagram. SE to run throughput benchmark on 4-GPU with three pipelines. Customer to provide 5k query trace and sample vectors. We'll meet week of 12/22 for results. Action items captured in the notes.
[15:24] Tom: Thanks all.
[15:26] Rajiv: Thanks.
[15:28] Meeting end.

Notes about transcription: filler words present, occasional mis-hears (K-V cash for KV cache), speaker overlaps.
